messages.subject: about phantoms cp="fa"
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
     May I check understanding for "phantoms". If I fit a two-factor CFA model, but suspect that there exist several minus factors (e.g., error covariances), shall I use "phantoms" approach to accommodate this situation (models are not perfect, it is realistic to have some error covariances but are not of major interest)? Or will you suggest using "add cross-loadings but with more diffuse priors" approach? Thanks!

Menglin

messages.subject: Re: about phantoms cp="fa"
messages.body_plain:
Menglin,

It sounds like residual covariances might be the way to go here. If you are using blavaan, the "phantom" thing is automatic, so you do not have to do anything special (besides specifying residual covariances in the syntax).

If you add cross-loadings, then you are saying that the observed variables are potentially related to the other common factor. But "minus factor" sounds like you are thinking about covariances that occur in addition to the common factors. Each residual covariance is roughly equivalent to adding an extra factor that only loads on two observed variables.

Ed

messages.subject: Question about dpriors()
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am running the following spline growth model,

BayesSpline.model <- '
i =~ 1*BSMMAT0199sm + 1*BSMMAT0103sm + 1*BSMMAT0107sm + 1*BSMMAT0111sm + 1*BSMMAT0115sm
s1 =~ -2*BSMMAT0199sm + -1*BSMMAT0103sm + 0*BSMMAT0107sm + 0*BSMMAT0111sm + 0*BSMMAT0115sm
s2 =~ 0*BSMMAT0199sm + 0*BSMMAT0103sm + 3*BSMMAT0107sm + 4*BSMMAT0111sm + 5*BSMMAT0115sm
i~~0*s1
i~~0*s2
s1~~0*s2
'
fitG8Mathbl <- bgrowth(BayesSpline.model,data=timssG8imp,burnin=5000,sample=100000,dp=dpriors(alpha ="dunif(300,400)"))
summary(fitG8Mathbl)

I need to provide a distribution for the intercept i, and so I used dp=dpriors() and specified a more informative prior on what I believe is the correct specification of the latent mean in GCM.  I am receiving the following error message.

Error : The following error occured when compiling and adapting the model using rjags:
 Error in rjags::jags.model(model, data = dataenv, inits = inits, n.chains = length(runjags.object$end.state),  :
  Error in node alpha[3,1,1]
Node inconsistent with parents

It may help to use failed.jags(c('model','data','inits')) to see model/data/inits syntax with line numbers
Error in blavaan(BayesSpline.model, data = timssG8imp, dp = dpriors(alpha = "dunif(300,400)"),  :
  blavaan ERROR: problem with MCMC estimation.  The model syntax and data have been exported.

Any thoughts would be helpful

Thanks,

David

messages.subject: Re: Question about dpriors()
messages.body_plain:
David,

I am guessing this happens because the starting value of alpha will be closer to 0, outside of the (300,400) bounds. Then jags chokes because the starting value of "alpha" is inconsistent with the prior. If you used a normal prior with almost all its density in (300,400), I guess it might work. Here are a couple other possibilities for getting it to work with the uniform prior (from easier to harder; hopefully easier works...):

1. Try the argument inits="prior".

2. lavaan has a start() modified that can be used in the model syntax, which might help you here (but there is a chance that it doesn't work in blavaan, I can't immediately remember).

3. Section 3.4 of the blavaan paper (URL below, should be appearing in J Statistical Software soon) provides some info on setting custom initial values "by hand".

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.05604.pdf

Ed

messages.subject: Bayesian MIMIC model: JAGS model from blavaan
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian MIMIC model: JAGS model from blavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

First off, great package and nice to see it being continuously developed and updated.
Consider the following simple two-factor multiple groups blavaan CFA model:

model.simple.twofac <- 'L1 =~ v1+v2+v3
                        L2 =~ v4+v5'

When looking at the generated JAGS model file (default priors), the specification makes a lot of sense:

model {
  for(i in 1:N) {
    v1[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,1], 1/theta[1,1,g[i]])
    v2[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,2], 1/theta[2,2,g[i]])
    v3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,3], 1/theta[3,3,g[i]])
    v4[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,4], 1/theta[4,4,g[i]])
    v5[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,5], 1/theta[5,5,g[i]])

    # lvs
    eta[i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu_eta[i,1:2], ibpsi[1:2,1:2,g[i]])
  }

  # mu definitions
  for(i in 1:N) {
    mu[i,1] <- nu[1,1,g[i]] + lambda[1,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,2] <- nu[2,1,g[i]] + lambda[2,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,3] <- nu[3,1,g[i]] + lambda[3,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,4] <- nu[4,1,g[i]] + lambda[4,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
    mu[i,5] <- nu[5,1,g[i]] + lambda[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]

    mu_eta[i,1] <- alpha[1,1,g[i]]
    mu_eta[i,2] <- alpha[2,1,g[i]]
  }

.....

}

The LVS' are assigned a bi-variate normal prior with mean 0 and Wishart prior for the variance-covariance matrix as per usual. However, I am looking to investigate the effect of a covariate 'age' on both the LVS', effectively turning the model into a MIMIC model:

model.simple.twofac.cov <- 'LV1 =~ v1+v2+v3
                            LV2 =~ v4+v5
                            LV1 + LV2 ~ age
                            LV1 ~~ LV2'

First, I have to specify LV1~~LV2 explicitly, otherwise, the covariance matrix is not estimated. Second, the resulting JAGS model file gives me a headache:

model {
  for(i in 1:N) {
    v1[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,1], 1/theta[1,1,g[i]])
    v2[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,2], 1/theta[2,2,g[i]])
    v3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,3], 1/theta[3,3,g[i]])
    v4[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,4], 1/theta[4,4,g[i]])
    v5[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,5], 1/theta[5,5,g[i]])

    # lvs
    eta[i,1] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,1], 1/psistar[1,1,g[i]])
    eta[i,2] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,2], 1/psistar[2,2,g[i]])
    eta[i,3] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,3], 1/psi[4,4,g[i]])
  }

  # mu definitions
  for(i in 1:N) {
    mu[i,1] <- nu[1,1,g[i]] + lambda[1,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,2] <- nu[2,1,g[i]] + lambda[2,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,3] <- nu[3,1,g[i]] + lambda[3,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
    mu[i,4] <- nu[4,1,g[i]] + lambda[4,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
    mu[i,5] <- nu[5,1,g[i]] + lambda[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]

    mu_eta[i,1] <- alpha[1,1,g[i]] + beta[1,3,g[i]]*age[i] + beta[4,1,g[i]]*eta[i,3]
    mu_eta[i,2] <- alpha[2,1,g[i]] + beta[2,3,g[i]]*age[i] + beta[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,3]
    mu_eta[i,3] <- 0
  }
......
}

>From the above model specification, we can see that a third latent variable is created (which turns out to be assigned a Normal(0,1) prior) which is then regressed on the latent variables alongside the 'age' covariate. The beta coefficient for eta_3 is defined as

  beta[4,1,1] <- sqrt(abs(lvrho[1,2,1])*psi[1,1,1])
  beta[5,2,1] <- (-1 + 2*step(lvrho[1,2,1]))*sqrt(abs(lvrho[1,2,1])*psi[2,2,1])

where 'lvrho' is defined as a function of a beta(1,1) prior

 lvrho[1,2,1] <- -1 + 2*parvec[6]
 parvec[6] ~ dbeta(1,1)

and 'psi' is an inverse gamma prior

 psi[1,1,1] <- pow(parvec[17],-1)
 psi[2,2,1] <- pow(parvec[18],-1)
 parvec[17] ~ dgamma(1,.5)
 parvec[18] ~ dgamma(1,.5)

There are a lot of different distributions interacting with each other. My question is: do you have any references regarding the way that the Bayesian multiple groups MIMIC model is specified? I am very curious since 1) there is not a lot of literature on the area and 2) I am uncertain whether this is a more complex way of specifying a simple model. I know that the JAGS model files created by blavaan are 'brute force' in the sense that a lot of the definitions are unnecessary (no loops etc.). So I am confused about whether creating a third latent variable is necessary for the estimation of the covariance between the latent variables when including predictors or whether the JAGS model is just complicating things. Unfortunately, I am not strong enough in matrix algebra to go through it manually with pen and paper, which of course would be ideal. So any pointers are greatly appreciated.

Best regards,
Sixten

messages.subject_clean: Bayesian MIMIC model: JAGS model from blavaan
messages.body_plain:
Sixten,

Re the explicit LV1~~LV2 specification: this may be related to the defaults of the command you are using (bcfa vs bsem vs blavaan). In general, blavaan does whatever lavaan does here. If blavaan does not do something that lavaan does automatically, that would be a bug and it would be helpful to see the command.

Re the jags code for the mimic model, all the general details are in this paper (in press at J Statistical Software):

https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05604

The short answer is that blavaan uses a method that improves the speed/efficiency of jags for many SEMs. The third latent variable is not necessary, but it allows us to use univariate normals in place of multivariate normals, and this can give a speed-up (not guaranteed for every model, but often is useful). If you want a general idea of what's going on, see Figs 1 and 2 of the paper. Basically, a covariance parameter is replaced with redundant parameters ("phantom" latent variables), in order to achieve conditional independence (allowing for use of univariate normals). MCMC allows us to move back and forth between an over-parameterized model and the model of interest.

Best,
Ed

> >     v4[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,4], 1/theta[4,4,g[i]])
> >     v5[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,5], 1/theta[5,5,g[i]])
> >
> >
> >     # lvs
> >     eta[i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu_eta[i,1:2], ibpsi[1:2,1:2,g[i]])
> >   }
> >
> >
> >   # mu definitions
> >   for(i in 1:N) {
> >     mu[i,1] <- nu[1,1,g[i]] + lambda[1,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,2] <- nu[2,1,g[i]] + lambda[2,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,3] <- nu[3,1,g[i]] + lambda[3,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,4] <- nu[4,1,g[i]] + lambda[4,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
> >     mu[i,5] <- nu[5,1,g[i]] + lambda[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
> >
> >
> >     mu_eta[i,1] <- alpha[1,1,g[i]]
> >     mu_eta[i,2] <- alpha[2,1,g[i]]
> >   }
> >
> > .....
> >
> > }
> >
> > The LVS' are assigned a bi-variate normal prior with mean 0 and Wishart prior for the variance-covariance matrix as per usual. However, I am looking to investigate the effect of a covariate 'age' on both the LVS', effectively turning the model into a MIMIC model:
> >
> > model.simple.twofac.cov <- 'LV1 =~ v1+v2+v3
> >                             LV2 =~ v4+v5
> >                             LV1 + LV2 ~ age
> >                             LV1 ~~ LV2'
> >
> > First, I have to specify LV1~~LV2 explicitly, otherwise, the covariance matrix is not estimated. Second, the resulting JAGS model file gives me a headache:
> >
> > model {
> >   for(i in 1:N) {
> >     v1[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,1], 1/theta[1,1,g[i]])
> >     v2[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,2], 1/theta[2,2,g[i]])
> >     v3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,3], 1/theta[3,3,g[i]])
> >     v4[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,4], 1/theta[4,4,g[i]])
> >     v5[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,5], 1/theta[5,5,g[i]])
> >
> >
> >     # lvs
> >     eta[i,1] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,1], 1/psistar[1,1,g[i]])
> >     eta[i,2] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,2], 1/psistar[2,2,g[i]])
> >     eta[i,3] ~ dnorm(mu_eta[i,3], 1/psi[4,4,g[i]])
> >   }
> >
> >
> >   # mu definitions
> >   for(i in 1:N) {
> >     mu[i,1] <- nu[1,1,g[i]] + lambda[1,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,2] <- nu[2,1,g[i]] + lambda[2,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,3] <- nu[3,1,g[i]] + lambda[3,1,g[i]]*eta[i,1]
> >     mu[i,4] <- nu[4,1,g[i]] + lambda[4,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
> >     mu[i,5] <- nu[5,1,g[i]] + lambda[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,2]
> >
> >
> >     mu_eta[i,1] <- alpha[1,1,g[i]] + beta[1,3,g[i]]*age[i] + beta[4,1,g[i]]*eta[i,3]
> >     mu_eta[i,2] <- alpha[2,1,g[i]] + beta[2,3,g[i]]*age[i] + beta[5,2,g[i]]*eta[i,3]
> >     mu_eta[i,3] <- 0
> >   }
> > ......
> > }
> >
> > From the above model specification, we can see that a third latent variable is created (which turns out to be assigned a Normal(0,1) prior) which is then regressed on the latent variables alongside the 'age' covariate. The beta coefficient for eta_3 is defined as
> >
> >   beta[4,1,1] <- sqrt(abs(lvrho[1,2,1])*psi[1,1,1])
> >   beta[5,2,1] <- (-1 + 2*step(lvrho[1,2,1]))*sqrt(abs(lvrho[1,2,1])*psi[2,2,1])
> >
> > where 'lvrho' is defined as a function of a beta(1,1) prior
> >
> >  lvrho[1,2,1] <- -1 + 2*parvec[6]
> >  parvec[6] ~ dbeta(1,1)
> >
> > and 'psi' is an inverse gamma prior
> >
> >  psi[1,1,1] <- pow(parvec[17],-1)
> >  psi[2,2,1] <- pow(parvec[18],-1)
> >  parvec[17] ~ dgamma(1,.5)
> >  parvec[18] ~ dgamma(1,.5)
> >
> > There are a lot of different distributions interacting with each other. My question is: do you have any references regarding the way that the Bayesian multiple groups MIMIC model is specified? I am very curious since 1) there is not a lot of literature on the area and 2) I am uncertain whether this is a more complex way of specifying a simple model. I know that the JAGS model files created by blavaan are 'brute force' in the sense that a lot of the definitions are unnecessary (no loops etc.). So I am confused about whether creating a third latent variable is necessary for the estimation of the covariance between the latent variables when including predictors or whether the JAGS model is just complicating things. Unfortunately, I am not strong enough in matrix algebra to go through it manually with pen and paper, which of course would be ideal. So any pointers are greatly appreciated.
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Sixten
> >
